title: When the Event happens, it simply happens.
subtitle: The surah opens on a certainty, not a maybe

row.title: when it comes
sub: a fact with a fixed time

then: The Makkan listeners found resurrection unbelievable and treated it as imagination. The surah does not open with an argument. It opens with {idea}When the Occurrence occurs{/idea}, a name for the Day chosen, Ibn Kathir says, because it is real and will surely come.
now: You plan in years: the mortgage, the retirement age, the kids' graduation. Death and the Day sit in a mental folder marked {trap}someday, maybe{/trap}. This verse moves them to the folder marked {idea}certain{/idea}.
old: The Day is something to think about later, if at all.
new: The Day is the one appointment in my calendar that cannot be moved.
try: Tonight before sleep, say one sentence to yourself about the Day as a fact, not a maybe.

title: When it comes, nobody will call it fake.
subtitle: No one can deny it, stop it, or take it back
then: In Makkah, denying the resurrection was easy talk. Ibn Kathir explains that once Allah commands the Day to begin, {idea}none can stop it or prevent it{/idea}. Qatadah said it will not be discontinued, taken back, or aborted.
now: Online, any fact can be called fake. You can scroll past, mute, block, unfollow. There is always another opinion. {trap}Denial works well, right up until the thing arrives.{/trap} That Day, nobody posts a counter-argument.
old: If I do not believe it, it does not really apply to me.
new: My doubt does not delay it by one second, so my preparation should not wait either.
try: Pick one thing you keep postponing because the Day feels unreal, and do a small part of it today.

title: The Day lowers some people and lifts others.
subtitle: Rank here is not rank there
then: Al-Hasan and Qatadah explained it: the Day {trap}lowers some to the lowest places, even if they were mighty in this life{/trap}, and {reward}raises others to the highest grades, even if they were weak{/reward}. In Makkah, tribal rank decided almost everything.
now: At work there is a clear ladder: the corner office, the intern, the cleaner who comes in after everyone leaves. You know where you stand on it. {idea}The Day uses a different ladder{/idea}, and people may swap places.
old: People's importance is roughly what it looks like from outside.
new: The quiet person I overlook may stand far above me that Day.
try: Thank one person today, by name, whose work usually goes unnoticed.

title: The ground you trust will shake like a sieve.
subtitle: The most stable thing you know becomes unstable

row.title: only Allah holds
sub: even the earth moves on command

then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said the earth will be {trap}violently shaken{/trap}, over all its surface and through its depths. Ar-Rabi bin Anas compared it to a sifter shaken with everything in it.
now: You have built your life on things that feel like solid ground: the job contract, the house, your health. Then one phone call or one scan result, and the floor moves. {idea}That small shake is a preview of what is not permanent.{/idea}
old: Some things in my life are simply stable and safe.
new: Even the ground under my feet holds only because Allah holds it.
try: The next time you feel your feet on the floor, say quietly: only You are permanent.

title: Even the mountains get ground down.
subtitle: The biggest thing you know is not permanent
then: To the Arabs, mountains were the picture of permanence. The tafsir says they will be {trap}relentlessly pulverized{/trap}. Ibn Zayd linked it to another verse that describes them as a heap of sand poured out.
now: The big company that seemed untouchable. The family name everyone respected. The career you thought was set for life. {trap}Things you called mountains{/trap} can fold in a year. {idea}What you did for Allah keeps its shape.{/idea}
old: If something is big and old enough, it will always be there.
new: If mountains crumble, my biggest worries and my biggest securities are both temporary.
try: Write down one thing that feels like a mountain to you right now. Under it, write: this too is temporary.

title: Mountains end as dust in the wind.
subtitle: Scattered, then gone without a trace
then: Ali described it as {trap}a rising dust storm that soon fades, leaving no trace{/trap}. Ibn Abbas likened it to embers rising from a fire that go out as soon as they land. Something huge becomes nothing at all.
now: Dust in a sunbeam through the window. You watch it float, then it is gone. Your trophies, your old profiles, the arguments you were so sure you had to win. {idea}A lot of it will end like that dust.{/idea}
old: The things I worked hardest for will leave a mark.
new: What looks heavy now can end as dust, so I should weigh what I chase.
try: Next time you see dust in sunlight, ask: will what I am doing today outlast this?

title: On that Day, everyone falls into one of three groups.
subtitle: Humanity sorted into three, not two
then: Ibn Kathir explains the three: those on the right, given their records in their right hands; those on the left, given theirs in the left; and {reward}the foremost, nearest to Allah{/reward}, fewer in number. He notes the end of the surah shows the same three at death.
now: Life sorts people all the time: grade bands, salary tiers, credit scores. You know how to move between them with effort. {idea}This sorting is already in progress{/idea}, one prayer, one kind word, one lie at a time.
old: I'm a decent person, so I will land on the good side somehow.
new: The sorting is happening in my ordinary choices, today.
try: Ask yourself honestly which group your last 24 hours point to. Then do one thing that points higher.

title: The people of the right: what a place to be!
subtitle: A question meant to make you long for it
then: The verse names the group and then asks about them, a way of saying {reward}how fortunate they are{/reward}. The tafsir says they are given their records in their right hands, and As-Suddi said they make up most of the people of Paradise.
now: You open an exam result and see the word that means you passed. Your shoulders drop and you call your mother. {reward}Being handed your record in your right hand{/reward} is that feeling, with no fear left.
old: Being among the right means barely scraping through.
new: The right is a place of honor, not a lucky escape.
try: Make a short dua today: O Allah, make me one of the people of the right.

title: The people of the left: how sad their state!
subtitle: The same question, with the opposite weight
then: The same form of question, now for those on the left, who receive their records in their left hands. Ibn Kathir calls them the people of the Fire and adds a short prayer: {trap}may Allah save us from their actions{/trap}. He prays against the deeds, not only the destination.
now: You see where a habit leads in someone else: the uncle and his temper, the friend and the debts. You know how it ends. {idea}The prayer is to be saved from the habits, while there is time to drop them.{/idea}
old: The left side is for other, worse people.
new: The road to the left is made of actions, and I can step off any of them.
try: Name one habit you would not want written in your record. Skip it once today.

title: Those who rushed ahead here are ahead there.
subtitle: The foremost in good stay foremost on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir says the foremost rank above those on the right and include {reward}the Messengers, Prophets, true believers and martyrs{/reward}. He links them to another verse about those foremost in good deeds by Allah's leave. The doubled word says it: first here, first there.
now: The group chat asks who can help someone move flat on Saturday. Someone always types me first, before thinking of excuses. {idea}That speed toward good{/idea} is what this verse honors.
old: I will get to good deeds once things settle down.
new: Being early to good is itself the rank.
try: The next time a chance to help comes up today, say yes first and work out the details after.

title: Their reward is to be brought near.
subtitle: Nearness to Allah is named before any garden
then: After naming the foremost, the verse gives their title before any garden is described: {reward}the ones brought near{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says they are in a better grade and nearer to Allah than those on the right.
now: You know the difference between a gift card from your manager and an hour where they really listen to you. One is nice. {idea}The other is being close.{/idea} The verse names closeness first.
old: Paradise is mainly about what I will get.
new: The greatest part is whom I will be near.
try: Spend two quiet minutes in sujood today asking only to be near Allah, nothing else.

title: Their home is the Gardens of Delight.
subtitle: Nearness comes with a place to live

row.title: the gardens
sub: the home that goes with it

then: The verses move from who the foremost are, to what they are, to where they live: {reward}the Gardens of Delight{/reward}. For listeners in the dry valley of Makkah, a garden was a picture of everything good.
now: After a long shift you come home, kick off your shoes, and the house is warm. That is the feeling of arriving. {reward}The Gardens of Delight{/reward} are the arrival after a life of striving.
old: My effort now leads to an uncertain end.
new: Effort toward Allah ends in a home, not in nothing.
try: When you get home today, pause at the door and ask Allah for a home in the Gardens of Delight.

title: Many of the foremost come from the early generations.
subtitle: The first believers set the pace
then: Scholars differed. Some said the earlier ones are earlier nations. Ibn Kathir preferred {idea}the earlier generations of this Ummah{/idea}, citing the Prophet's ﷺ words that the best people are his generation, then the next, then the next.
now: You read about people who believed when it cost them family and safety. Your faith costs you an early alarm. {idea}They set the pace{/idea}, and the door they walked through is still open.
old: The great believers lived back then. That race is over.
new: Their example is a pace to follow, not a closed chapter.
try: Read one short story about an early Muslim today and take one habit from it.

title: Only a few of the foremost come later.
subtitle: Being first to good gets rarer, so it counts more
then: Ibn Kathir explains the later ones as {idea}the later generations of this Ummah{/idea}. Among them, the foremost are {trap}few{/trap}. Abu Hurayrah reported that this news was hard for the Companions when it was revealed.
now: In a packed stadium, a few people still stand up at the back to pray when the time comes. Few is not zero. {idea}A few means there is a place, and someone will take it.{/idea}
old: If only a few make it to the front, it won't be someone like me.
new: A few will be from the later ones, and I can aim to be one of them.
try: Choose one good deed most people around you skip, and do it quietly today.
